meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The single biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Bernard Shaw. The line traces to Fortune journalist William H. Whyte in 1950; the Shaw credit first surfaced in 1994.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — traces to William H. Whyte
answer.sourceLine: The idea traces to journalist William H. Whyte, who wrote in Fortune (September 1950): “The great enemy of communication, we find, is the illusion of it.” The polished modern wording evolved over decades of retelling, and was pinned on George Bernard Shaw only in 1994 — with no evidence Shaw ever said it, per Quote Investigator ↗.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: The great enemy of communication, we find, is the illusion of it.
trail: 1950: William H. Whyte, in Fortune’s “Is Anybody Listening?”, writes “The great enemy of communication… is the illusion of it” — the earliest documented form, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1950s–70s: the phrase circulates, often unattributed or credited to a garbled “William White,” while the wording drifts toward “the illusion that it has been achieved,” per the same chronology ↗.
1994: a business/TQM textbook first attaches the line to George Bernard Shaw — 44 years after Shaw’s death, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Today the Shaw credit is repeated everywhere, including in the press, e.g. The Irish Times ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ Whyte’s 1950 original — the familiar “single biggest problem… illusion that it has taken place” is a later paraphrase
source.excerptNote: Whyte’s Fortune line is the seed. Over the following decades the phrasing drifted — through variants like “the greatest barrier to communication is the illusion that it has been achieved” — into today’s smooth aphorism, per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.
source.rightsNote: The polished modern wording is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase with no fixed author; William H. Whyte’s original 1950 Fortune text is a copyrighted work. Treat the aphorism as of uncertain rights rather than public domain.

author.name: William H. Whyte
author.heading: Who was William H. Whyte?
author.bio: William Hollingsworth “Holly” Whyte was an American journalist and organizational analyst who joined Fortune magazine in 1946. Writing about corporate communication, he coined the “illusion of communication” idea in a 1950 article, then became famous for his 1956 bestseller The Organization Man. In later life he turned to studying human behavior in public spaces, producing works such as The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980).

misattribution.heading: The Shaw problem
misattribution.intro: The line is near-universally credited to George Bernard Shaw — on quote sites, in slide decks, and in the press. The credit is a late invention.

items.why: No work, letter, or speech by Shaw contains the line. The Shaw credit does not appear until 1994 — 44 years after his death — in a business/TQM textbook, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Mid-century reprints mangled Whyte’s name into “William White” or “William H. White,” muddying the trail back to the real author, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented source is journalist William H. Whyte in Fortune, September 1950 — not George Bernard Shaw, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Shaw
lead: The aphorism is a magnet for misattribution because it is witty, epigrammatic, and about communication itself — exactly the register readers associate with George Bernard Shaw, the era’s reigning wit. Whyte’s plainer 1950 original, buried in a corporate-communication article, lacked that polish.

As the wording was smoothed over decades into its current memorable shape, it drifted toward the most famous plausible name. By the 1990s the Shaw label was self-reinforcing: each quote site copied the last.
context.pull: A blunt observation about corporate PR, gradually reshaped into a Shavian epigram.
